subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING SYSTEM

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. C-170 respecting employer and employee relations in the public service of Canada-Mr. Pearson-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 2-Definitions.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING SYSTEM
speechtext:
Several months have passed, Mr. Chairman, since the house gave second reading to this bill, No. C-170, an act respecting employer and employee relations in the public service of Canada and to the related measures, Bill C-181, an act respecting employment in the public service of Canada and Bill C-182, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act, and referred them to the special joint committee for the purposes of study and report. My brief remarks at this time relate to all three measures, and it is not my intention to speak on clause 2 of the other two bills.
The special committee under the joint chairmanship of hon. Senator Bourget and the hon. member for Ottawa East has applied itself with great diligence and patience to a very important task. I am sure I voice the feelings of all the hon. members of this committee when I express the gratitude of hon. members to this special joint committee for the study they have given all three bills.

DEBATES	February 17, 1967
Previously the committee had reported on an act to amend the various superannuation acts, and has now had referred to it the matter of pensions paid to retired civil servants or their dependants. However, this latest reference to the committee is not in any way related to this legislation or to the reports made by the committee arising out of its consideration of these bills.
The reports of the committee on Bills C-170, C-181 and C-182 are set forth at pages 1259 to 1281 of Votes and Proceedings for February 3, 1967, where all amendments recommended by the committee are to be found. In addition the committee has ordered all three bills reprinted as amended, and these are now in the hands of all hon. members.
The committee held many meetings. Representations were heard from all associations and organizations representing civil servants, and from the central labour bodies and other interested groups. I think it can be said that the fullest hearing has been accorded to all those who have an interest in the public service. A great deal of effort has gone into the drafting of these measures and into the studies associated with their preparation. To this effort the committee has added its own very careful and very thorough study. I thank the hon. members of this house and those of the other place for their thoughtful work and the contribution they have made to this legislative program.
I know hon. members would want me to extend a special word of thanks to the joint chairmen. The proceedings took place in an atmosphere of calm reflection and deliberation. This is to the credit of the chairmen, its members and this parliament of ours. I believe there was no other interest in the minds of all hon. members except the interest of the people of Canada and their concern to ensure, as far as can be assured through legislation, that Canadians in the years to come would be well served by their public service.
I want to make clear now that the government is pleased to accept the amendments proposed by the committee to the bills. As we proceed in committee of the whole on the clauses of the bills those clauses will be called as amended, and I hope accepted, because in my view they strengthen the measures previously placed by the government before this house.
e (11:30 a.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during my years in parliament few bills have
February 17, 1967	COMMONS
been presented to this house of more basic importance or lasting significance. Indeed, a more intricate and complex bill would be difficult to imagine.
The bill has had a most detailed study in the joint special committee, and in my view its passage through the committee of the whole need not be greatly delayed. The bill which has been returned from the committee is very greatly improved over that which was given second reading in this house. It is still far from ideal, and without doubt additional amendments and improvements will be required in the years ahead.
The immensity of the task of introducing a system of collective bargaining for the determination of pay and conditions of employment in the public service is well indicated by the statistics of total employment with the federal government. The latest available statistics were published in January of this year and are for July, 1966. Total employment with the federal government in July of 1966 was 372,890, of whom 223,850 were employed in departments or departmental corporations and 149,040 were employed in proprietary, agency or other federal corporations. It appears, therefore, that about 225,000 public servants are directly affected by this bill, and there can be no doubt that the pay and conditions of employment of the other 150,000 employed by crown corporations will be indirectly but very materially influenced.
The President of the Treasury Board has commented upon the work of the joint special committee. Personally I have never been a member of a committee which worked more harmoniously, more assiduously and with more complete freedom from political partisanship. That is as it should be. The public service of Canada is an immense credit to the nation. I suggest there is no public service anywhere in the world which exceeds the Canadian service in dedication, responsibility or ability, and there are many, many branches of the public service of Canada which are unequalled anywhere in the world in scholarship, accomplishment or achievement.
I am not generally in the habit of paying compliments publicly to hon. gentlemen opposite. Too often I have found such references to be treasured and used at the time of the next election. Nevertheless, I cannot in justice refrain from paying my respects to my friend of long standing, the hon. member for Ottawa East, for his role and attitude as Commons chairman of the joint special committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING SYSTEM
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Public Service Collective Bargaining

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING SYSTEM
speechtext:
His intelligent guidance of the committee, his firm, dignified but pleasant presiding manner made work on the committee a pleasure, and I thank him for it.
I only hope it may help to win for him the long overdue reward of moving his office to the east wing of this building where he may join the Senate chairman. I can say that because I think it would make the role of the party to which I belong much easier in Ottawa East.
The magnitude of the committee's work is best illustrated by the fact that during some 39 sittings a total of 182 amendments were made to the bill, as I count them. I think this must be something of a parliamentary record. Of the 182 amendments, I calculate 49 are of substance and greatly improve the bill originally presented to the house. A better justification for the committee system could hardly be found.
Much of the credit for the improvement in this bill belongs to those who presented briefs. Those briefs were studious and informed. Those of the staff associations reflect great credit upon the calibre of the leadership and research qualities of these organizations. The assistance of such distinguished public servants as Dr. George F. Davidson, Arnold
D.	P. Heeney, Q.C., Mr. J. D. Love and Mr. P.M. Roddick was invaluable.
Despite this, Mr. Chairman, I remain unconvinced that the government has chosen the wisest course in the presentation of this bill. In my view a better and a wiser course would have been to undertake a complete revision and modernization of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and the inclusion therein of a separate part reflecting the different circumstances in the public service. The closer the provisions for collective bargaining in the public service are brought to provisions for the private sector, the better it will be for both, I am convinced.
There is no doubt that without substantial amendments the I.R.D.I. Act would not immediately meet the needs of the whole public service, though it might well apply to the post office as it does to crown corporations today. But the act, that is the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, is in my view out of date for the private sector and is in most urgent need of revision to conform to modern thinking in industrial relations. It would have been much better to revise that act and divide it into three parts; first, the general sections which would apply across the board to the public service and the private
13160	COMMONS DEBATES	February 17. 1967
Public Service Collective Bargaining sector alike; second, those provisions which by their nature are applicable only to the private sector under federal jurisdiction. The third part would be those provisions which by their nature are applicable only to the public service.
Several of the briefs before the committee made vigorous representations that an amended I.R.D.I. Act and not this bill should be used. Notable among these were the briefs of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, the Letter Carriers Union of Canada, the Canadian Labour Congress, and the lithographers and the typographical unions. I have considerable sympathy with their submissions. However, the die is cast otherwise and I raise the matter only to say this. No doubt as a result of the study by the task force headed by Dean Woods a modernization of the I.R.D.I. act will be undertaken by parliament within the next two or three sessions, if not earlier. By that time there will have been experience with this bill. Its deficiencies will likely have been disclosed. At that stage I believe the government then in office should give careful consideration to the consolidation of the I.R.D.I. act and this bill into a new three part employer-employee relations code applicable in the manner I have suggested to both the private sector and the public service.
The success of the present bill, C-170, will be largely dependent upon the calibre and qualities of the public service staff relations board. I urge upon the president of the Treasury Board and the government to spare no pains to obtain as chairman and vice chairman persons of the highest excellence. Reports are circulating that the chairmanship will be offered to Professor Jacob Finkelman. I hope the rumours are true, because I believe there is no man in Canada more scholarly and enlightened yet more down to earth and practical in the field of employer-employee relations than Professor Finkelman.
Equally, Mr. Chairman, the initial stages of this legislation will require of the bargaining agents a high degree of responsibility and what I may describe as employer-employee statesmanship. Without it bickering, unrest and loss of morale in the public service could be the result.
A major improvement in the bill, without which I could not support it at all, was the complete revision made in relation to the time the bargaining agent must choose between compulsory arbitration or the alternative of conciliation with the right to strike. In the bill as originally drafted this election had to

be made before certification, a time when the election might well be mischievous. The new provisions permit the delaying of election until immediately prior to the commencement of negotiations, clearly a time when the will of the employees themselves is most likely to be known.
The committee was confronted with a grave problem in respect of the rather considerable number of employees in a managerial or confidential category who will be excluded from the operations of this bill. In fact these employees, numbering many thousands, would be in a less favourable position than at present, since they will be deprived of their existing right of consultation pursuant to section 7 of the Civil Service Act, without being brought under this bill and the provisions of collective bargaining.
The special joint committee has strongly recommended the establishment of an advisory committee on the model of the standing advisory committee for the higher grades in the public service in Great Britain. Before this bill clears committee, we on this side of the house will expect a specific and unequivocal commitment from the President of the Treasury Board that the government will establish such an advisory committee.
This leads me to submit that there is still a useful and constructive role for the national joint council. That council has many substantial accomplishments to its credit. I believe it can still perform a most valuable service for all public servants in fields not covered by collective bargaining; for example, superannuation. Before the committee stage of this bill is concluded we shall expect a statement of the government's intentions in respect to the future of the national joint council. o (11:40 a.m.)
Then, sir, I wish to draw specific attention to the recommendation to the joint special committee as follows:
Your committee recommends that the government consider legislation to continue the pay research bureau and to provide for the data collected thereby to be available to the bargaining parties under Bill C-170.
I have perhaps a paternal interest in this bureau, because one of my first acts on election to this parliament was to urge its establishment. I succeeded in this urging. It was first established in 1957 on the recommendation of the gentleman for whom I then served as parliamentary assistant, Hon. Donald M. Fleming, minister of finance. Despite some growing pains and some shaky techniques at
February 17, 1967	COMMONS
the outset, the bureau has been of tremendous value in the process of pay determination. I think it is most urgent that in the future there be impartial and factual research about comparability of salary and wage levels in the public service with equivalent categories in private industry. The results of this research, I submit, must be available equally to the bargaining parties. I ask the minister to give the committee an unequivocal undertaking that the government will carry out this recommendation of the joint special committee.
I believe it is of special interest to members of parliament that under this bill the staffs of the Senate, the .House of Commons and the library of parliament are excluded. The joint special committee has recommended amendments to the Senate and House of Commons Act, the House of Commons Act and the Library of Parliament Act to provide to these employees rights and advantages similar to those which this bill provides. I confess to some surprise that the President of the Treasury Board has not already arranged the introduction of such amendments to these three acts so they could be considered in association with this bill. I ask the minister to make clear at once the intentions of the commissioners on internal economy and of the government in this regard. The employees in this building must not be placed in a position less favourable than that of other public servants. I submit the amendments to the three acts should be introduced at once and enacted at this session.
During the hearings of the joint special committee the question was raised-and I pursued it-of the inclusion in the bill of a so-called conscience clause to permit the exclusion of those persons who on grounds of religious belief or training object to membership in a bargaining agency or to the payment of fees or dues thereto. It is true that the number of such persons is small, but there is a basic principle involved. In a number of other jurisdictions the matter has been settled by the inclusion of a conscience clause which would permit the objector to make a contribution to an approved charity of an amount at least equal to the fees or dues that otherwise would be payable. I do urge the minister to adopt the model contained in the Saskatchewan act of 1965 as amended in 1966. If he does not do so I propose to test the opinion of the committee of the whole by an amendment at the appropriate time.
Public Service Collective Bargaining
The most unfortunate by-product of this legislation is the red circling program. Without doubt collective bargaining requires a simplification and rearrangement of the 700 classes and 1,400 grades which there have been previously in the public service. But in reducing the number of classes to something like 70 the government has brought a grave injustice to thousands upon thousands of civil servants, and has created more unrest and loss of morale than at any previous time ever existed in the public service. I deplore the way in which the red circling was carried out. What I am unable to comprehend is how the Civil Service Commission can be so confident that its present reclassification program is correct, when all it does is overrule and set aside classifications made by that very commission in years gone by. How is it that the commission made so many mistakes-indeed, 10,000 mistakes-in earlier years but has now achieved infallibility? It is the ordinary civil servant who is being made to pay for those alleged mistakes on the part of the Civil Service Commission.
Again, I strongly suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that the only fair way to settle this red circling fiasco-and that it is-is to exempt incumbents completely and permit them to have and enjoy all the advantages which would have accrued to them had their position not been red circled. The reduction in classification would become effective when the position was next filled, when the successful applicant would accept the position with his eyes open.
Red circling is not the only headache there will be in the institution of collective bargaining. There will be other complications and other growing pains. No doubt this bill will require amendment from time to time. Collective bargaining will not create a new valhalla for public servants. But in this day it is inevitable and desirable. I intend to support this bill, with reservations in respect of certain clauses which I shall express when we reach them. My earnest hope is that under collective bargaining the government of Canada will prove to be a model employer, and that the enactment of this bill will accrue to the advantage not only of public servants but of all Canadians.

I also want to say a word about the work of the committee. In recent months a good many members of parliament have indulged, as I have-this includes several members of the government and, if I remember correctly, the hon. member for Hochelaga has written about it-in the exercise of calling for a revision of the rules and procedures of parliament in order to bring our work more in consonance with modern requirements. There was no better example, it seems to me, of one of the ways in which parliamentary procedures can be improved than the work of this committee and other committees on which I have served and about which I have been told. It has always seemed to me that when we sit around the table at a parliamentary committee meeting we become a great deal less partisan than we are on the floor of this house. In committee we tend to be much more concerned with the merits of the subject matter before us than with taking positions and stances that are intended for some kind of political projection.
I urge that we learn from the work of these committees and try to find ways of not only handing more important legislation to the committees but of ensuring that the work done by the committees is not repeated on the floor of this house and in committee of the whole, as has happened in the case of one or two bills. I have learned that in committee, much more than in the house it is possible to persuade the government to accept changes if one has reasoned arguments to support them. It is much easier, at least, than persuading them to accept changes in this chamber. I am confident that we can improve the work of this parliament a great deal by not only extending the functions of parliamentary committees but giving those committees powers which they do not now have and arranging our parliamentary rules in such a way that the work of committees, as I have said, is not repeated on the floor of this house.
I am not going to try to cover all the points of this bill. I think the minister was right, and perhaps he understated the position, when he said the bill had been improved by the special joint committee. In my view having taken, as he knows, together with my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Carleton
February 17, 1967	COMMONS
and other members of the committee a very active part in seeking changes, Bill C-170 as it now lies before the members of this committee bears hardly any resemblance in basic principle to the bill which the government originally presented. The changes which have been made are not merely changes of detail or procedure. In every case the amendments that were made, and which the government members on the committee accepted, let me add-the remark I am making is not partisan-were changes of fundamental substance, which now make this bill closer to a genuine collective bargaining bill than it was when first introduced.
Having paid a compliment to the officials of Treasury Board, let me now say something which may not be as complimentary to them.
I found in dealing with them in the committee that the original approach of the government and the officials had been to grant the public service employees collective bargaining but to fence it around in such a way that it really would be no more than a shadow of any real collective bargaining process. There was obviously a fearfulness on the part of the officials, which no doubt reflected the attitude of the government, that if there were full collective bargaining the whole thing would run amok, and they wanted to be sure there were limitations here and limitations there, with every "i" dotted and every "t" crossed in such a way that nothing would have been left for real collective bargaining.
It is therefore a great tribute to the officials and those who instructed them to say that when we were able to persuade them, in most cases, of the value of some fundamental change they later came back with wording appropriate to meet the request which was made. I repeat that the bill now before this committee is entirely different in basic principle from that which appeared before us on second reading. That is why, despite the fairly severe criticisms representatives of my party made of the original bill, we will support this bill and its companion bills with much greater happiness than we could possibly have done before.
I have still several very serious reservations about the bill. If committee members will permit me to refer to it, I would say that I had occasion to spend a day last Wednesday with a large group of representatives of the Public Service Alliance, postal employees and others interested in this legislation. I went over with them, so far as I could, some of the
Public Service Collective Bargaining matters that will be concerning them in practical negotiations on the basis of these bills. They informed me that Dr. Davidson and Mr. Love, as well as the President of the Treasury Board, had met with the group the day before.
I suggested to them, as I say to the committee now, that there are still some serious difficulties about this bill on which they ought to keep a very careful eye. If the practice shows that those difficulties are real, it will be the duty of this parliament to make the necessary amendments to overcome them. The first difficulty-and I do not put these forward in any order of importance-is represented in the clause now before the committee and on which these general statements are being made. The wording of the exclusions is still extremely broad. It will be easy for the employer to abuse his powers if he wishes to do so. It will be easy for the employer to seek exclusion to such an extent as to remove from the process of collective bargaining thousands of men and women who ought not to be removed from it.
I am very concerned about the breadth of the language in many of the subclauses of clause 2 of the bill. We discussed them at great length in the committee. If I may make a personal reference, I sometimes felt I was making myself an extreme nuisance to the other members of the committee by insisting and digging in my heels on a number of points in this clause, as in others. We made some important changes in this clause, but to my mind some parts of the clause are still far too wide.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
Whether the broad wording will in fact be a disservice to the collective bargaining process and to the excluded individuals will depend on the integrity and care with which the employer-in this case the government, or according to this bill, the Treasury Board -will seek to interpret the broad language used in clause 2.
I agree with the hon. member for Car-leton-he and I both raised the matter before the committee-that in view of the fact that literally thousands of public service employees will be excluded from the process of collective bargaining under the heading of managerial and confidential employees, it is of the greatest importance that the recommendation of the special joint committee that a special advisory committee be set up to deal with the government in relation to the terms
13164	COMMONS
Public Service Collective Bargaining and conditions of work of such excluded personnel be carried out by the government.
In order to ensure that the government would not use its usual language, namely "we will do it soon" and-"soon" is the most elastic word I have ever heard since I have been on the floor of the house, a word which may mean anything from one to 100 years-I moved that the committee unanimously accept a time limit on this recommendation specifying that the government is to establish this advisory committee within six months from the time these bills are passed. We will watch very carefully to see whether the government will in fact act within six months to set up this committee to deal with the thousands of excluded personnel as a result of the practical application of the bill now before the committee.
However, I am a great deal more disturbed about another matter which I asked members of the house to consider very carefully. We will not move any amendment to these bills on this point either at this stage or at any stage because we have reached the conclusion-and I may say that the people whom I met last Wednesday told me they agree fully with this approach-that the important thing is to get these laws into action as quickly as possible and with the least possible delay, so we may acquire a year or two of experience under these laws. If changes are necessary we will be able to make them on the basis of practical experience rather than attempting to foretell what may happen. My concern stems from the fact that a huge and important area of normal employer-employee relations is excluded from collective bargaining under Bill C-170 and its two companion bills, C-181 and C-182.
I am referring to the areas of classification, appointment, promotion, demotion, lay-off and release of employees. For example, the red circling fiasco to which the hon. member for Carleton referred would not have arisen if there had been collective bargaining on the question of classification. In every case with which I have had some experience where reclassification has taken place the union, if it was strong enough, was able to achieve the result which I suggested in a few questions to the President of the Treasury Board some months ago and to which the hon. member for Carleton referred in his speech this morning, namely that the red circle rates should not apply to incumbent employees. I suggested that the incumbent employee should continue to receive the old rate and all the increases
DEBATES	February 17, 1967
given to other employees, and that the red: circle rates should apply only to a new employee in the particular position affected. This is the only way to deal with red circling,, because otherwise the government is punishing an employee by unilaterally changing the understanding on which the employee accepted the job. This problem would not have arisen if there had been collective bargaining on classification.
I am very worried that the largest part of job opportunity and job security is excluded from collective bargaining. The reason we finally decided, after many hours of argument, to let it take its course and see how it works, and the reason we were given for the exclusion of this area from collective bargaining, was the desire to maintain the merit, system and to ensure that only the Civil: Service Commission, or the public service commission as it will be called, will have any authority in making decisions and setting, standards with regard to the merit system.
I was not convinced of that at that time and I continue to be unconvinced that it is impossible to bring these areas within collective bargaining and at the same time guarantee that the merit system will continue. I am unconvinced that it is impossible to wed the merit system to seniority, length of service and all the other aspects of job security sought by employees. I continue to feel certain that it would have been possible to do so, but the officials of the department and the representatives of the Civil Service Commission insisted that it was not.
Therefore we decided, and I hope the future will show it to be a wise decision, to let. it go for the moment and see how it will work in the next two years. However, let me reiterate to the President of the Treasury Board and to his negotiating officials that this is an area which worries the public service employee representatives more than any other section in the present bills. To give a simple example, they are deeply concerned that on Monday they may negotiate with the government and reach an agreement on a certain rate of salaries, and on Tuesday have that rate eroded by unilateral reclassification in the same way the-red circling has affected employees without the right of collective bargaining. This is-what has happened on many occasions in private industry.
Therefore let me be presumptuous enough-as to say to the President of the Treasury Board and his officials, as well as to the public service commission to be set up, that if

February 17, 1967	COMMONS
those bodies so apply the unilateral exclusive right of classification and appointment of employees, etc., as the law as it is presently worded permits them, and thereby irritate the public service employees, this collective bargaining process will be in danger the day after it begins.
I urge those in the government who are responsible for collective bargaining to make absolutely certain that every avenue of consultation, information, appeal and discussion be explored so the employees concerned are persuaded that they will not suffer as a result of this exclusive power in the hands of the authorities, and as a result of the exclusion of this important area from negotiation.
As I said on second reading of this bill, I continue to be worried about the powers given to the staff relations board and the numerous duties that have been laid upon it, those of certification, of deciding what is to go to conciliation after the negotiations have broken down, of dealing indirectly with adjudication, and a whole host of other responsibilities and duties. I still have a strong feeling that the board will encounter a great deal of difficulty in the practical working out of its functions. Since we were dealing with a field which had not been previously tried it was thought wiser, after drawing these difficulties to the attention of those responsible, to hang one's doubts on the clothes line for the next year or two and see how the staff relations board works out in practice.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre shares these doubts and reservations. I am still very unhappy over the lack of appeal open to an employee dismissed for alleged security reasons. The old section of the Civil Service Act was brought into a companion bill without, in my opinion, sufficient amendment. It is true that after some discussion a provision was inserted providing for a hearing, although the details of that hearing are not put into legislation. This is somewhat of an improvement. I still feel deeply unhappy, however, about the fact that anyone can be dismissed for any reason without being able to appeal to some independent body and have his day in court. We did not press this much further than the amendment we obtained, and which now provides for a hearing, in the hope that the cases will be so infrequent and the actions of the authorities will be so definite and well grounded there will be no injustice in fact.
Public Service Collective Bargaining
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think I have covered the points I wanted to make. I want to deal with only one final point. After a great deal of discussion about political activities of public servants we were finally presented with a proposition the fullness of which is found in Bill No. C-181 but which leaves us in this party dissatisfied. I have never been able to understand, and I cannot understand now why, subject to certain exceptions, the public service employees should not enjoy the full political freedoms and rights that other citizens of the country enjoy. I just cannot understand it.
I was disturbed beyond words, Mr. Chairman, last Wednesday when I met with a group of the leaders of the public service of Canada and discussed this question of political rights. A leading spokesman said at that meeting that one of the reasons public service employees are not particularly anxious about political rights is not that they do not want them but that many civil servants are afraid that if they are given political rights some of their superiors will demand that they exercise them in a certain direction. Apparently there is a fear about this in the public service which must be widespread. I cannot say from my own experience that this is so, but it must be widespread or this particular gentleman who holds an extremely important position in one of the public service organizations would not have made that statement in the presence of 90 or 100 other leaders of public service employees.
I regret there is this fear amongst employees of the federal government that if they are given such rights some misguided superior, some irresponsible superior, will insist that they exercise those rights in the direction of one political party or another. I am not saying this merely to be friendly or courteous, but if that is the case I am sure it is not the fault of this government or the immediately preceding government, although I am equally sure it is the fault of governments in the past when patronage controlled appointments and promotions in the civil service. This tradition has persisted, and I think it is shameful that it should continue.
One of the ways to remove this fear is to give the people concerned full political rights, and give them protection. In some ways this bill does give protection against discrimination for exercising or failing to exercise political rights. I want to emphasize before
13166	COMMONS
Public Service Collective Bargaining this committee, as we had occasion to emphasize again and again before the special joint committee, that those of us who urge full political rights for public service employees are not saying the bill should require them to belong to a party or support a party. This is not what is before parliament or the public service employees. What is before us is the removal of an inhibition that the law previously contained. Civil servants will be as free to be just as apathetic about their political duties as the rest of the people of Canada so frequently are. There would be no compulsion that they exercise the rights which would be given. There would be provision merely that if they wanted to exercise them they could do so.
The proposal which was made to us and which is contained in Bill C-181, Mr. Chairman, contains one absurdity and one humiliation. The absurdity is that this proposal provides that a public service employee may make a contribution to a political party or attend political meetings but he is prohibited, not in so many words but in the total provision, from being a member of a political party. Later one finds he is permitted to apply to the public service commission for permission to be a candidate for a political party. I do not know very much about the constitution of other parties in this parliament, but I would be very surprised if the Liberal party, the Conservative party, the Social Credit party, the Ralliement Creditistes or the independent party, if there is one, were different from the New Democratic Party on the point that before you can be a candidate you must be a member. Certainly our constitution provides it. I am told the Conservative party constitution provides that, and I would be surprised if the Liberal party constitution did not have a similar provision.

Mr. Chairman, while not having had the privilege of serving on the committee that dealt with the legislation now before us I must say that, having watched the progress which has been made, and upon examining the bill before us which has been amended, reprinted and reported by the joint committee, can only be impressed by the tremendous amount of constructive work that has been done. For this the committee is to be commended; certainly the bill now before us is much more satisfactory than the original
February 17, 1967
one. Likewise, Mr. Chairman, we would express our appreciation of the fact that the President of the Treasury Board has stated here today that it is the policy of the government to accept the various amendments which have been agreed to in committee.
I wish to speak on a very limited area of this legislation today. I believe that, apart from this general area, most of the amendments that have been made and which improve this bill meet with the approval of the members of this party. Nevertheless I am inclined to say something which I think is basically important about which the bill does not satisfy us, and in regard to which in my opinion there must be further amendments to strengthen the bill.
The hon. member for Carleton referred to the fact that he intends to move a conscience clause. May I say that we in this corner of the house will give our fullest support to such an amendment, because it is imperative that it be included in the bill. While the bill does set out very clearly the right of public servants to collective bargaining, unless this particular aspect is properly taken care of in this legislation I think this provision will work a very grave injustice upon many members of the public service and will thus be detrimental to the service itself.
It is in this vein that I should like to continue my remarks, and I begin by posing several questions which I think must be answered. What really is the meaning and actual scope of freedom of assembly, freedom of association and freedom of religion as declared in the Canadian Bill of Rights? What is the result of allowing the employer and the union, the employee organization, to include in a collective agreement a provision which in effect intimidates and/or threatens and/or compels an employee to continue to be a member of an employee association?
I would further ask, Mr. Chairman, what protection does the government offer to civil servants who for various reasons, religious or political, cannot in good conscience join with and financially support a particular employee organization? Does it mean that one only has the freedom to do what the majority tells one to do? What does freedom of association actually mean as far as the bill of rights is concerned if compulsory membership in an employee organization is a requirement of this bill?
I would further ask whether the government intends to issue an order to all its
Public Service Collective Bargaining employers, its agencies, boards and commissions should this bill become law as it is presently framed, instructing them to safeguard Canadians rights to freedom of association, freedom of religion and freedom from coercion, compulsion, discrimination and intimidation. While this may seem to be a very minor aspect of this bill, Mr. Chairman, it is of vital importance to the well-being of all Canadians and to the perpetuation of the traditional way of life that we in Canada regard as so important.
I should like to refer very briefly in this connection to the provisions of the Canadian Bill of Rights. The preamble to the act reads:
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of family in a society of free men and free institutions;
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law;
And being desirous of enshrining these principles and the human rights and fundamental freedoms derived from them, in a bill of rights which shall reflect the respect of parliament for its constitutional authority and which shall ensure the protection of these rights and freedoms in Canada:
It was on this basis that the bill of rights was enacted, Mr. Chairman, and everyone in the house at the time voted in support of it. There are a few sections of this act to which I should like to make reference as they relate to this particular problem that the bill before us presents. Section 1 in part I reads as follows:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,
(a)	the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;
(b)	the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law;
(c)	freedom of religion;
(d)	freedom of speech;
(e)	freedom of assembly and association:
That last provision is the one which gives me concern for this bill, Mr. Chairman. Freedom of association also carries with it the implication that there shall be freedom not to associate. It was former Governor General Vincent Massey who said:
Freedom always faces dangers. A free people remains free only through daily acts of courage. A nation's bravery in war cannot atone for timidity in time of peace. We deny our freedom if we do not speak when there is something to be said.

13168	COMMONS
Public Service Collective Bargaining
It is support for this thought that causes me to speak in this vein today. We want loyalty and dedication in our public service, and I believe we have it now. I would agree that we have one of the finest public services of any free country in the world. As Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
Freedom breeds loyalty. Coercion always was the mother of rebellion.
I believe that if we are to preserve the loyalty and perpetuate the dedication that we have in our public service at the present time we must be very careful to enshrine in the legislation that we pass in this house basic freedoms which, in my opinion, would include the right of freedom to associate as well as freedom to dissociate.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I mention another thought in this regard. Section 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights says:
Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared,-
Section 3 says:
The Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the Privy Council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons, in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part and he shall report any such inconsistency to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.
I ask the President of the Treasury Board whether this legislation has been referred to the Minister of Justice, to comply with the section of the bill of rights I read. Unless we have the assurance of the Minister of Justice that the provisions of the bill before us are consistent with the bill of rights, we have failed in our examination of this bill.
I urge that before this bill is given final passage we refer it to the Minister of Justice. The bill of rights was passed; we support it as being right. This bill should be consistent with the bill of rights especially with section 3 of part 1 of the bill of rights. I ask that the present bill be referred to the Minister of Justice. We want him to see whether clause 8(2) (c) is consistent with section 3 of the bill of rights. It is vitally important.

I draw the attention of the committee to another important declaration of human rights. Last December I was privileged to be at the United Nations when the universal declaration of human rights was given final passage through the assembly. The United Nations had worked on this matter for 20 years, in draft form. It had been the basis of the agreement that each country made when it became part of the United Nations. I do not intend to go over the entire declaration of human rights; that is now part of the constitution of the United Nations in its final form. I merely want to refer to one or two sections. The preamble says:
Whereas recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world ...
Whereas member states have pledged themselves to achieve, in co-operation with the United Nations, the promotion of universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms-
Article 1 says:
All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
Article 18 says:
Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion; this right includes freedom to change his religion or belief, and freedom, either alone or in community with others and in public or private, to manifest his religion or belief in teaching, practice, worship and observance.
1 mention clause 18 because it is a conscience clause, and relates to clause 8(2)(c) of the bill before us.
Article 20 says:
(1)	Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.
(2)	No one may be compelled to belong to an association.
If this legislation compels every member of the public service to belong to a specific or specified association, it contravenes article 20 of the universal declaration of human rights.

The formula proposed in this amendment is one which has been used in other jurisdictions. I would point in particular to the trade union act of the province of Saskatchewan enacted in 1965 and amended in 1966. Under that legislation it is possible for someone who states that he conscientiously objects, on grounds of religious belief and training, to joining a trade union or to paying the dues of a union pursuant to the Rand formula, to contribute an equivalent amount to a charity or charities which may be approved by the labour relations board of that province.

I will refrain at this stage of the proceedings from explaining to the committee my inner thoughts on that matter. But I say it, as I will on every occasion, because I have heard hundreds and thousands of workers, and even labour leaders, say how they are flabbergasted to see that the governments have not set up the required machinery so that, in the last analysis, they would not have to strike as the only way to solve their problems.
Besides too many strikes today are only a way to blackmail the governments concerned. I do not think that it is in the interest of the common good. As a matter of fact, even a large number of workers who are involved in those strikes are beginning to realize that public opinion has had enough.
I am not saying those things to blame necessarily the strikers who must fall into line when the movement gets under way. They undoubtedly realize that in most cases there is no other solution than a strike. On the other hand, because they are personally involved and their own interests or those of their families are affected, they feel that those strikes are costly in the end. And for whom? For those who go on strike. They become the first victims of such a strike and, in most cases, that strike does not bring them any tangible benefits.
Then, I wonder whether something should not be added in the legislation-again, such action might be premature on examination of this bill, since it appears to have gone through a long and complicated procedure, and I am under the impression that most of the members of the house do not wish to delay its passage-that the majority seems ready to try it for a period of one or two years, at the risk of having to introduce amendments next year. However, I submit that among such amendments, one should aim at creating, and this for the public service more than for any other sector, machinery capable of restricting as much as possible

Let us consider teachers, a very topical subject right now. I think most school boards would like to give teachers the right to strike or to choose compulsory arbitration. This is a very confusing and provocative subject and school boards have not quite resolved their differences with school teachers. These differences should be resolved by agreement.

It is not true in all cases that people in the private sector have the same security and benefits as those guaranteed under the public service statutes. Therefore the two sectors cannot be considered in the same way. One cannot treat them equally for one purpose and forget about their difference for another. Therefore, I do not wish to prolong the debate on this section needlessly. On the other hand, I have just heard remarks, from the member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings as well as from the member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) with which I disagree so wholeheartedly that I feel I must express my disapproval.
Of course, it is easy at the present time, because of certain crises which have affected Canada as a whole and certain provinces in particular, to speak of the right to strike as if it were a sort of plague. The right to strike, at the present time, in the eyes of many people, is not very popular. Quite naturally, one goes
Public Service Collective Bargaining along with a prevailing trend in public opinion at this time by claiming that the right to strike is above all else, dangerous and that any legislation should first of all protect, or if I may say, vaccinate the public weal against eventual strikes.
I am surprised that the right to strike is not considered in the same manner as most members of this house view other rights which are just as fundamental, such as, for instance, freedom of expression, freedom of speech, and the right of representation. I should like to emphasize here that the right to strike is a hard-won victory by workers and wage-earners.
It is also a fundamental right in a democracy that the right to strike should not be tampered with any more than freedom of expression. I know that some strikes can bring about unpleasant results; I also know that the right to strike can lead to abuse, but I must point out that unpleasant results and abuse can ensue from any of the fundamental freedoms for which members of this house are always ready to fight, except for this one perhaps.
As for me, I find quite natural that this bill should recognize the right to strike as a normal right and it is therefore granted until an exception proves necessary in the case of the public service. They would have us take the opposite view and say that the right to strike is the exception, whereas the rule would be to restrict such right to strike. I feel this latter attitude is unacceptable. The former should prevail and this is precisely what is provided for in the bill we have before us.
I doubt very much that the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) was in order when he tried to have the house believe a minute ago that union leaders were people who toyed with strikes as with some sport, that they benefited from strikes in all sorts of ways, such as having their pictures in the papers while the unfortunate strikers were the ones to suffer from almost every strike. I feel that if the remarks of the hon. member were out of order, any comments of mine would also be out of order but they may be tolerated in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres.
I feel that an entire concept is being developed in this direction. The member for Trois-Rivieres said that he was on the picket, lines. I congratulate him for that. I wonder if: he ever tried to tell a whole group of striking workers thay they were being victimized by their union leaders at that time.

I suppose that that is an understandable position for a Conservative to take, but it is a little sad to see that attitude so rigidly taken by one so relatively young in years and of considerable figure.
I think the hon. member came dangerously close to building a case for saying that he is against people, though I do not think that any one of us in this house who know the hon. member would seriously believe that that is so. However, he was attempting to express feelings that he has, and I think his remarks did reveal that in our society today we are in a state of flux, that there is room for questioning in which particular direction we should go in an increasingly complex society to keep society on the rails, and at the same time preserve the rights and freedoms of individuals. This much I think was revealed by the remarks of the hon. member, and to

that extent I give him full credit for voicing his views.
I think that if most of us in this house were honest, Mr. Chairman, we would agree that there is a great deal of room for questions to be asked in this particular field, and that neither in this legislation nor probably in the report that the Woods committee brings in will we have any final and necessarily lasting answers as to how we should proceed in this matter.
At the moment, Mr. Chairman the point at which I differ from the viewpoint expressed by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings is that this is a most opportune time for us to be doing a little bit of trail blazing. While perhaps some of the provisions in this particular area are not ideally what I should like to see, nevertheless I think a little bit of experimenting in this field-if that is indeed what it is-is not something for which the Canadian government should be condemned but rather something which should give us as Canadians cause to be proud that we are prepared to do some venturing and searching into this field, which I think all of us agree is a complicated one, and in many ways fraught with uncertainties.

If we firmly believe that the people of the world are sufficiently educated to sit down and settle their differences and prevent wars and poverty in various countries, surely we can expect they are sufficiently educated to solve domestic problems. that the right to strike was banned. Of course that is not the case. Arbitral tribunals are available in Britain under the aegis of the Whitley Councils and there is no prohibition of the right to strike. There is silence on the subject. Unless we take the position that a strike is treasonable, which I think is unlikely, there is no reason to take the position that the right to strike for public servants is unlawful in Britain today. Under existing legislation in Canada there is silence; there is neither recognition of nor prohibition against the right to strike for public servants.
Those who have suggested this afternoon that in this legislation we are extending recognition of the right to strike are approaching it in the wrong way. What the legislation in effect does is provide a technique for compulsory arbitration and also provide a technique for conciliation. Those who take the road to conciliation retain the right they now have to strike. That is all that is happening under this legislation. This legislation then goes further and in clause 79 gives the right to the governor in council to designate certain employees who shall be called "designated employees" whose duties consist in whole or in part of duties the performance of which at any particular time or after any specified period of time is or will be necessary in the interest of the safety or security of the public.

I dissociate myself completely from those people who are prepared to say that civil servants do not have the ordinary rights of other citizens of this country. He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing second reading of Bill C-28 which is entitled an act respecting the Canada Court of Indian Claims I can best sum up its basic principles by referring the house to my remarks which may be found on page 2178 of Hansard of March 3, 1966. At that time we were considering the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and I said that the fundamental issue in our relationship with the Indian people in Canada is "whether we of European ancestry are going to be able to hold up our heads before them".
I submit that this is the basic principle involved in the bill. Following that suggestion,

which I made in the debate at that time, I went on to recite some of the history of the legislation concerning Indian claims in more recent times. At that time I said:
On December 14,	1963 the then Minister of
Citizenship and Immigration introduced Bill C-130, An Act to provide for the Disposition of Indian claims. As members of the committee will recall this bill had its genesis in the joint committee on Indian affairs which brought out a report in 1961; but Bill C-130 after a preliminary stage in the house, was circulated widely throughout the country, and then on June 21, 1965 we had a successor bill. Bill C-123, which was to have been referred for consideration last fall to a special committee for detailed consideration.
At _ this time arrangements were under way for the appearance of Indian people and others before that committee, until the bill, along with a number of other things, came to an untimely end with the dissolution of parliament. I might also draw the attention of the committee again to the fact that in addition to the bills introduced on the government side, to which I have referred, there was in 1963 Bill C-67, entitled An Act Respecting the Canada Court of Indian Claims, introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Skeena.
I may say that the terms of Bill C-28 which we now have before us are identical to those of the bill previously introduced by my colleague.
Having made reference to the various bills that have been brought forward I would like to express the view that the exact terms of any of them including the one which we have before us, are relatively unimportant. What is really important to me is the settlement of a moral issue, that is the restoration to the Indian people of self respect and, perhaps even more important to many of us, the restoration of our own self respect in our relationships with the Indian people. In my view the purpose of such legislation must be to create a situation in Canada where we will no longer be haunted by the injustices perpetrated by our forefathers, which I think we all recognize cannot really be undone, but which in my view can be removed in so far as they are still being visited upon the children of this day and generation.
The important thing to me is to bring about a state of affairs where we and the Indian people can look one another fairly and squarely in the eye, where we no longer need to speak and they no longer need to fear that we will be speaking with a forked tongue. I recognize fully the fact that legislation alone cannot achieve this end, but I do believe that legislation can act as a catalyst to bring about this end. I submit that if this end, which to me is one of the most desirable and important
February 17, 1967

objectives to which this country should be moving, is to be achieved, the basic contents of the legislation that may be put forward in this parliament is not unimportant.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It is no secret, Mr. Speaker, that in my view the legislation which has been introduced by the government so far has been to put it mildly, less than satisfactory for the purposes that I suggest we should all have in mind. My views in this regard are perhaps best spelled out by an amendment which I moved to government Bill No. C-123 when it was before the house on June 22, 1965. This amendment can be found in Hansard on page 2768. At that time I moved, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That Bill C-123 be not now read a second time, but that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation that will provide for
(a)	an Indian Claims Commission enabled by its terms of reference and its composition to assist the Indian peoples of Canada to prepare for disposition of all outstanding claims arising out of the occupation by non-Indians of territories now within Canada; to search out and hear evidence in relation thereto and to make such awards, both general and particular, as are just and fair, and
(b)	an Indian Claims Appeal Court, the presiding officer of which shall be a jurist, other than a Canadian citizen, of international repute, which shall hear appeals from any decision of the commission.
I believe that principle is in this bill, although rather awkwardly put because of the limitations that are imposed upon a private member, since he does not have the prerogative of financial initiative that the government has. What I believe is implicit in this bill and in the amendment I previously moved is, first, that prior recognition of the fact that claims do in fact exist must be given, and such claims should not be subject to narrow restrictions such as whether they arise from actions of the Crown in right of Canada, or of any of the colonies which preceded the Canadian confederation. These claims should not be subject to the restriction of whether they arise from the actions of corporations such as, for example, the activities of the Hudson's Bay Company or other fur trading companies, or from the actions taken by individuals under what they assumed to be rights conferred upon them under Canadian or other laws, or actions they may have taken outside of the law.

The second thing, Mr. Speaker, which I believe is implicit in the principle of this bill is that the claim must be dealt with as if negotiations were being conducted between equals. This is something which was not done in the past. At that time a superior power simply moved in with all the trappings of imperial colonialism. Since that time there has never been any real acceptance of this idea of negotiations between equals. Ever since the successful encroachment of imperial colonialism into this continent, the relationship between the Indian people and ourselves, both in the state and in a large part as individuals, has been a sort of father-child relationship. The actions of this parliament, indeed the actions of the Fathers of Confederation, in effect created this father-child relationship by making the Indian people legal wards of the federal government of Canada.
It may be argued with some truth, Mr. Speaker, that in recent years the father has become a bit more generous. He has not restricted the child entirely to a diet of cold porridge. He has been prepared to hand out occasionally a few lollipops and perhaps even on occasion what one might term a full bodied meal of meat and potatoes. This basic situation has not been altered in any way by the events which may have transpired because this parliament has been fit to provide the government with somewhat more generous amounts of money to dispense to the Indian people across the country. I submit that handouts are not the answer. More and more the Indian people are no longer content to be treated as adult children. I believe that more and more of us are realizing the futility of attempting to play over and over again the role of father. I believe that negotiations by an Indian claims commission would be the key which could unlock this paradoxical situation in which we and they have involved for far too long.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) on the presentation he has made of a very interesting case. One of the frustrations that we in this house have had to put up with for some time now has been the fact that before this parliament and the government has moved to change the direction we are taking in Indian affairs, we have submitted the proposals to the Indians themselves for their deliberation and approval.
I think that this is a very good move, but it is also very frustrating because we see a great many abuses and needs which must be met which we cannot deal with as quickly as we would like, because of this outstanding prior necessity for getting the consent of the people concerned. This is going to slow the activities of the government and of the House of Commons in the matter of legislating for the Indians. However, I think it is all to the good and it is a very forward looking step to allow the Indians to have a greater say in the legislation which governs them.
One of the interesting comments that was made by the sponsor of the bill was that although he thought the bill might be deficient in some respects he felt that the principle of the bill should be discussed. To some extent, Mr. Speaker, I disagree with this view, and I should like to take a look at the
February 17, 1967

contents of the bill itself. It is not really enough to suggest that the end is justified unless we take a look at the means. Therefore I should like to make a somewhat academic analysis of a variety of provisions contained in the bill, with a view perhaps to clearing up some of the ambiguities which now exist.
I think that one of the first objections one could make to the bill is one which we are continually coming across in private members hour, and it is, of course, that the bill contemplates the expenditure of public moneys. We are all aware of the well worn phrase to be found in citation 249 of Beau-chesne's fourth edition, which reads in part as follows:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
There are several clauses in the bill Mr. Speaker, which presume to do exactly this. Perhaps the most outstanding is clause 19 which deals with the procedure of the court to be set up under the bill, and with the payment, in whole or in part, of the reasonable costs, fees, or expenses of preparing and presenting a claim or an interest affected, the court being empowered to order that such expenses, either in whole or in part, may be the administrative expenses of the court.
Additionally, Mr. Speaker, the expenditure of money by the judge who would be required if the court were to come within the ambit of the Exchequer Court would have application here, as well as the increased salaries, money required for travelling and administration extra staff and so on.

My hon. friend says Indians in Canada. But Indians are not defined. Does my hon. friend mean Indians or the band? What happens if there is a conflict between the rights of the band and those of individual Indians? Much will depend, of course on the different land holding procedures that exist and, of course, these vary from place to place.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Whose interests are to be paramount? Is it the interest of the band or the individual? There are 550 odd Indian bands in Canada, and this should be spelled out in more detail so that when the court deals with these matters there can be no difference of opinion and everybody will know who may bring a claim.

I also wish, to refer to subclause 2 of clause 14. This clause permits the court to hear and determine claims submitted to the court by petition concerning Indians or lands reserved for Indians. Questions must be answered about this. Who may petition? On whose behalf may the petition be lodged? How many are required to submit a petition? Must these people be Indians, or can it be somebody outside the band? For example, can somebody outside the band submit a petition on behlaf of a dissident group within the band who do not appreciate the way things are going?
In this connection I wish to mention something to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. We ran into this when we visited the St. Regis band, which is having difficulty with its elected members.
Because of the situation there,-and the band has been handling some of its own affairs for some time-there has been created a great deal of confusion and a great deal of bad will between two conflicting parties within the band. To avoid such conflicts and to protect the people concerned, this matter should be more precisely spelled out. For instance, can anyone petition on behalf of Indians? We have been objective with legislation covering the rights of Indians with respect to land reserved for Indian use. But this clause to which I have referred is wide open, and the matter is not precisely defined. The objections I previously raised apply to this clause.
Continuing, we find that there is no definition, no basis on which a claim might be lodged. This is not spelled out in detail, and raises problems which should be looked into. For example, the clause as presently drafted does not allow the Indians concerned or the court set up in this bill to determine what classes of claims might be brought to the court. As an example of this in clause 14 (1) paragraphs (a) and (b), which deal with British Columbia land question and the Oka land dispute, neither of these particular things is defined.
It may be perfectly natural for somebody coming from British Columbia to know precisely what is meant by these disputes, but somebody coming from my part of the country might not know about them. It is not fair to assume that the court will know. The bill might have been improved had the hon. gentleman opposite defined more clearly what is meant by these particular paragraphs. I admit that in a legal sense the courts might

know what is meant, but I doubt whether this is so.
As a result there are intriguing possibilities when it comes to interpreting the legislation. First, dealing with the three clauses I have referred to, does it mean that any Indian claim, any individual claim no matter how frivolous or ridiculous it may be, must be considered by the courts? Must it be considered equally with more substantial claims launched by other individuals or bands? Second, does the band have precedence, or a superior status with respect to claims started by an individual? This should be resolved one way or the other. Third, can the individual act when the band council does not act? For example, in a case where a legitimate claim is outstanding and where the band has reasons of its own for not taking action, would an individual resident of the reserve be allowed to take action to settle his claim?
Another aspect I wish to raise is, whether individuals and bands can submit claims on one particular matter? That is, can the band and other persons acting individually submit claims to the court? These questions are not resolved in the bill and they cause much confusion. They should be more clearly defined, so that the people petitioning the court and the court itself may have a better understanding of the rights and privileges involved.

Let me speak of precisely how this bill fits in with the general principle of that commission. The progress we make with respect to that commission is slow. A great many claims in my constituency are to go before the commission. It has not yet

been set up, and has not been operating because the various Indian groups in Canada, as I understand it, cannot agree about how it should be set up, what its powers should be and how it should operate. When you begin to deal with Indian affairs you learn about the vast diversity of opinion among the various Indian groups across Canada. Many Indian bands such as the Caughnawaga and St. Regis bands, which the members of the Indian affairs committee visited last week, are relatively able to look after their own interests. Those two reserves that we visited are well able to do without the Department of Indian Affairs in many respects. Perhaps in five or six years it might be possible to withdraw Indian affairs service from those people. They can manage on their own.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This very diversity hampers the government, the House of Commons and the standing committee when dealing with Indian affairs. It makes it difficult to lay down a policy which will apply equitably across the board, taking into consideration the variations which exist, as well as the educational opportunities for integration into Canadian life. The claims commission is a perfect example. There are a variety of claims to be processed, one of which is the exotic series of claims from the west coast about which I do not claim to have much knowledge. But I do know that the claims we have to face arise from a variety of natural causes, as well as from the plain skulduggery of many of our ancestors.
I know that in my own constituency treaty No. 3 has been broken because it was necessary to use the watershed of the lower Rainy River as storage for power. Thus, many areas which were once part of the mainland have become islands and have been lost to the Indians. They were taken over by the Crown and sold to summer settlers. Much land has been lost, some of it valuable.
There are also the leases which were signed in the early part of the century for what was then considered to be a fair price. Today the fair price is no longer fair. For example, under one lease seven bands receive $35 for a considerable territory. In 1905 when the lease was signed this may have been a good deal, but in 1967 it is not a good deal. I think that in the future the Indian claims commission will have to look into these old leases which were signed in former days in good faith by both parties but which are no longer equitable in 1967.
