I recognize the difficulty which has developed; the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and I have been allied closely on this particular measure, as with other measures, for some years. I realize that I run the risk of talking out my hon. friend's bill, since at any moment there may be a knock on the door to tell us we are required in the Senate chamber. I have often wondered why we have to put up with these interruptions-why they cannot take place after six o'clock-but that is the way things are.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). I wish you had not called him to order, Mr. Speaker, during his comments about the intimate parts of this bill because it was obvious that the hon. member was niggling around the subject, not getting to the core of it. It is interesting to note that when he was dealing clause by clause with the bill now before the house he complained about its vagueness and generality. Then, when he began to talk about the Indian claims commission as the subject matter of the government's proposal in this regard he stressed the difficulties which arose because of differences across Canada between one region and another, and explained why it was not possible to get a clear picture of the claims made by the Indian people.
I submit that when he made his later remarks dealing with the position of the government he answered his own question and gave a perfect explanation of the reason for drawing up this bill in its present form. It is not possible to clarify a great many of these matters, so they were left open to the court itself.
I think I might usefully give an historical account of what has occurred with respect to the subject of Indian claims in this nation, and begin by referring to a pamphlet published by the Liberal party during an election

February 17, 1967
Indian Affairs
in 1963. It begins by saying that at Prince Rupert in 1910 Sir Wilfrid-presumably Sir Wilfrid Laurier-promised that the Indian land question would be taken to the Privy Council. Then the pamphlet adds: "The solution in 1963 lies in a totally different course of action". This emphasizes the attitude of successive parties with regard to the land question in British Columbia and in a broader sense to all the claims Indians have advanced with respect to encroachment upon their rights, their traditions and their land. If it is considered as a milestone in the development of our approach to the claims of the native people to refer back to a promise broken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier 50 years ago, there is surely something wrong with the attitude of successive governments in dealing with these matters.
I wish, now to make a comment on the land question in British Columbia because this is a question of vital importance not only to the Indian people in that province but to the government and to all of Canada. I think this is separate from a large number of the claims which the native people have to present about various aspects of the treatment which has been meted out to them. In 1910 it was considered that Sir Wilfrid Laurier or his government would assist in solving the land question. Obviously no solution was reached at that time. In 1926 a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons met to consider what I believe was called the claims of the allied native tribes of British Columbia. That committee concluded that the native people had not proved their claim to aboriginal title. They did not say it was disproved; they simply said it had not been proved. In any event, it recommended a payment of $100,000 a year to the native people of British Columbia. That payment is still being made but it has been greatly diluted as a result of a population increase among the native people, and because of the reduction in the purchasing power of the dollar.
In the late '40's a committee on Indian affairs was established and it delved into many aspects of Indian problems. In 1948 it unanimously recommended that an Indian claims commission be established. Nothing was done about this recommendation, which was supported by members of all political parties represented on the committee. It was forgotten. In 1959 another committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was formed to consider Indian affairs. In 1961 that
committee made its report, and again representatives of all parties in the house and in the Senate unanimously recommended the establishment of a court of Indian claims or of an Indian claims commission, I forget which. That committee specifically referred to the British Columbia land question and to the Oka land dispute, and as a consequence these matters are referred to in the bill now before us.
On October 14, 1963, Bill No. C-130 was introduced to establish an Indian claims commission. The intention was principally to introduce the bill at that time-parliament was close to prorogation-in order that copies might be distributed to the Indian people in Canada and to all others who were interested. It was distributed and many representations were made about changes to the bill. Contrary to what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has said,-and I looked over these representations-there was a considerable body of opinion among the Indian people in Canada that there were great deficiencies in the measure introduced in 1963.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In June of 1965 another bill was introduced, known as Bill C-123. It was almost identical to Bill C-130 and obviously had no regard for that body of opinion among the native people which had been expressed during the examination of the earlier bill introduced in 1963. This fact prompted the Indians of the North American Indian Brotherhood to form a group called the Federation of Indians of British Columbia. The prime function of that group related to the Indian land question. That brotherhood had, among other things, the following to say about the last bill introduced by the government:
It is considered by the Indians of the North American Indian Brotherhood to be an insult on the part of the then Minister of Indian Affairs the Honourable Jack Nicholson to then reintroduce the bill in the old form except for one minor change, namely that there be provision for one Indian to sit on the commission. All the recommendations except this one, by both the N.A.I.B. and the other Indian organizations of B.C. were disregarded and the N.A.I.B. considers the amended bill in most of its entirety to be absolutely useless in giving to the Indians of B.C., according to the Liberal pre-election promise an "unbiased and unprejudiced tribunal."
Those are not my words but the words of the North American Indian Brotherhood.
Mr. Speaker, someone is knocking at the door so I must cease and desist.
